title: The menstrual cycle and how to verify the phase
goal: Describe the hormones and phases of the menstrual cycle in plain words, and say how a study should verify the phase and why many do not.

steps.title: Two halves, one ovulation
steps.text:
The [menstrual cycle](g:menstrual-cycle) is counted from **day 1, the first day of bleeding**, to the day before the next bleed. Research treats 21–35 days as normal [[c:fem-eumen]].

[Ovulation](g:ovulation), when an ovary releases an egg, splits it in two:

- the **[follicular phase](g:follicular-phase)**: bleeding until ovulation;
- the **[luteal phase](g:luteal-phase)**: ovulation until the next bleed.

The brain hormone [LH](g:lh) drives the ovaries, and they make [oestrogen](g:oestrogen) and [progesterone](g:progesterone). Regular bleeding is not enough to call a cycle healthy: *eumenorrhoea* needs ovulation too. A cycle with bleeding but no ovulation is an [anovulatory cycle](g:anovulatory-cycle).

claims.text: Research defines eumenorrhoea as 21–35 day cycles, at least 9 periods a year, an LH surge and a correct hormone profile.

evidence.quote: Define eumenorrhea as menstrual cycle lengths ≥ 21 days and ≤ 35 days resulting in 9 or more consecutive periods per year, plus evidence of LH surge, plus correct hormonal profile

steps.title: What the hormones do across the cycle
steps.text:
A research guide by Elliott-Sale and colleagues picks four time points that differ clearly in hormones [[c:fem-profiles]]:

| Point | When | Oestrogen | Progesterone |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | bleeding, up to day 5 | low | low |
| 2 | about a day before ovulation | highest | low |
| 3 | ovulation (positive [ovulation test](g:ovulation-test), 24–36 h) | medium | low |
| 4 | about 7 days after ovulation | high | highest |

The LH surge triggers ovulation. After it, progesterone climbs and peaks about a week later. What differs between points is the level of each hormone and the balance between them.

claims.text: Four points in the cycle (bleeding, just before ovulation, ovulation, a week after ovulation) have clearly different oestrogen and progesterone levels.

evidence.quote: Capture the lowest concentrations of oestrogen and progesterone
Capture the highest oestrogen concentration, while progesterone remains low
Capture a medium oestrogen concentration, while progesterone remains low
Capture the highest concentration of progesterone and a high concentration of oestrogen

steps.title: Verifying the phase

claims.text: A study of the effect of cycle phase needs biochemical confirmation of the phase, with cycles tracked for at least 2 months.

evidence.quote: biochemical confirmation of the phase is warranted alongside self-reported menstrual characteristics
Track and establish menstrual cycle characteristics for ≥ 2 months prior to testing.
Reduce unfounded assumption that ovulation, and thus eumenorrhea, has been established

claims.text: Some women have menstrual bleeding without ovulation (anovulatory cycles).

evidence.quote: Define anovulatory as those who experience menstruation but do not ovulate

steps.title: Why many studies fall short

claims.text: The vast majority of high-quality sport science data come from studies with men.

evidence.quote: the vast majority of high-quality sport and exercise science data have been derived from studies with men as participants

claims.text: Differing hormonal profiles may explain the mixed findings of studies with women.

evidence.quote: it is reasonable to assume that the heterogeneic findings observed among studies conducted with women as participants, particularly those examining physiological responses to exercise and adaptations to training, may be attributable to the numerous hormonal profiles a woman may experience during her lifetime

claims.text: The meta-analysis of menstrual cycle phase and performance rated its evidence as low quality.

evidence.quote: The quality of evidence for this review was classified as "low" (42%).

points: Day 1 is the first day of bleeding; ovulation splits the cycle into a follicular and a luteal phase, and normal cycles last 21–35 days.
Oestrogen peaks just before ovulation; progesterone peaks about a week after it. Bleeding alone does not show that ovulation happened.
A good cycle study tracks cycles for 2 months or more and confirms ovulation and hormone levels, not just a day count.
Many studies assume the phase, pool different hormone profiles and have low quality, so their mixed results are shaky.

variants.stem: Which day is day 1 of the menstrual cycle?

options.why: Right: cycles are counted from the first day of bleeding.
Ovulation comes mid-cycle; it splits the cycle in two but does not start it.
Bleeding lasts several days; the count starts on its first day.
The LH surge comes just before ovulation, around the middle of the cycle.

variants.stem: What event divides the follicular phase from the luteal phase?

options.why: Right: the follicular phase runs up to ovulation, the luteal phase after it.
Bleeding starts the cycle and the follicular phase; it does not separate the two.
Progesterone peaks inside the luteal phase, about a week after ovulation.
The end of one cycle is the start of the next follicular phase.

variants.stem: A runner bleeds every 28 days. She has never had an ovulation test or a hormone blood test. Which description is safest?

options.why: Right: regular bleeding is a sign, but ovulation has not been shown.

options.text: Eumenorrhoeic, because her cycles are regular
options.why: Eumenorrhoea needs ovulation and a correct hormone profile, not only regular bleeding.
Amenorrhoea means periods are missing; she bleeds every 28 days.

options.text: Anovulatory, because no test was done
options.why: Without a test you cannot say she does not ovulate either; it is simply unknown.

variants.stem: At which point of the cycle is progesterone highest?

options.why: Right: progesterone peaks in the middle of the luteal phase.
Both hormones are lowest in the first days of bleeding.
This is the oestrogen peak; progesterone is still low.

options.text: At the moment of the LH surge
options.why: Progesterone climbs only after ovulation has happened.

variants.stem: A cyclist is tested in the lab within a day of a positive ovulation test. Which hormone pattern fits best?

options.why: Right: at ovulation oestrogen is below its peak and progesterone is still low.
That is the pattern of the first days of bleeding.
That is the pattern about a week after ovulation.
Oestrogen peaks just before ovulation, while progesterone is still low.

variants.stem: A study wants the biggest contrast between high oestrogen with low progesterone and high progesterone with high oestrogen. Which two points should it compare?

options.text: Just before ovulation, and a week after it
options.why: Right: the first has the top oestrogen with low progesterone, the second the top progesterone.

options.text: Early bleeding, and just before ovulation
options.why: Early bleeding has both hormones low, so progesterone barely differs between the two.
Neither has high progesterone, so the progesterone contrast is lost.

options.text: Early bleeding, and a week after ovulation
options.why: This contrasts low and high on both hormones, not the oestrogen/progesterone balance asked for.

variants.stem: Which home test can show the LH surge that comes just before ovulation?

options.why: Right: it detects the LH surge in urine.

options.text: Counting 14 days from the last period
options.why: Counting assumes ovulation, it does not detect it.
Heart rate is not a validated test of the LH surge.
Apps predict from past dates; they do not measure a hormone.

variants.stem: A study tested 12 runners on day 21 of their cycle, counted from the last period, and called it the mid-luteal phase. What is the main limit for conclusions about the luteal phase?

options.text: Day counting does not show ovulation or progesterone level
options.why: Right: the phase was assumed, not verified, so some runners may not have had a luteal profile.

options.text: Twelve runners is too many for a lab study
options.why: Small samples are the usual problem, not large ones, and sample size is not the phase problem here.

options.text: Day 21 is always too early for the luteal phase
options.why: Timing depends on cycle length and ovulation date; no day is always wrong.

options.text: Running tests cannot detect luteal effects
options.why: Nothing about running tests blocks this; the weakness is the unverified phase.

variants.stem: A triathlete bleeds every 30 days for a year, but her blood progesterone stays low in the second half of each cycle. What does this suggest?

options.why: Right: bleeding without the post-ovulation progesterone rise points to no ovulation.
Regular bleeding alone does not show ovulation, and her hormone profile is wrong for it.
Amenorrhoea means periods are missing; she still bleeds.

variants.stem: Why are results on cycle phase so hard to compare across studies?

options.text: Phases are defined in different ways and ovulation is often unchecked
options.why: Right: the same label can cover different hormone profiles.

options.text: Female hormones are too small to measure
options.why: They can be measured by blood tests; many studies just did not.

options.text: Women's performance changes at random from day to day
options.why: Day-to-day variation exists in everyone; the problem here is unreliable phase labels.

options.text: Women rarely volunteer for lab studies
options.why: Recruitment is hard, but it does not explain the mismatched phase definitions.

variants.stem: A review pools "luteal phase" results from 10 studies. Six set the phase by counting days, four by blood progesterone. What is the main problem for the pooled result?

options.text: It mixes verified and unverified phase definitions
options.why: Right: one label then hides several hormone profiles.

options.text: Ten studies is too many to pool
options.why: More studies usually help; the problem is how the phase was set.
Blood tests are the more reliable method.

options.text: Pooling always hides a real effect
options.why: Pooling can show or hide effects; here the issue is the mixed phase definitions.

variants.stem: A reader sees that studies found no performance difference between phases and concludes the cycle never matters. What is the best reply?

options.text: Too early: phases were often unverified, and averages hide individuals
options.why: Right: weak methods and averages can hide real effects in some women.

options.text: Correct: no group difference means no effect in any woman
options.why: Averages can hide individual differences.

options.text: Wrong: the studies hid a large effect on purpose
options.why: Nothing suggests this; the weakness is method, not bias.

options.text: Correct, but only for strength, not endurance, outcomes
options.why: The same limits apply to endurance and strength studies.
